mmlu.oneSentence: MMLU measures broad multitask knowledge across many academic and professional subjects using multiple-choice questions.
coreIdeas: A single score can hide uneven capability, so the benchmark spans many domains and difficulty levels.
The benchmark is useful because it asks whether models transfer knowledge across subjects without task-specific training.
Accuracy is easy to compute, but interpretation still depends on contamination, prompting, and subject mix.
mmlu.whyItMatters: MMLU is the canonical example of a broad knowledge eval. It helps Phase 0 separate simple exact-match mechanics from the harder question of what a benchmark actually covers.
mmlu.phaseConnection: Use it while designing the phase0-core suite: group questions by skill, report category-level results, and avoid treating one aggregate number as the whole story.
suggestedReadingFocus: How tasks and subjects are selected
How few-shot prompting changes the measurement
Where the authors caution against overinterpreting aggregate accuracy

humaneval-codex.oneSentence: The Codex paper introduces HumanEval-style functional correctness testing for generated code.
coreIdeas: Code generation should be evaluated by executable tests, not just text similarity.
pass@k captures whether any of several samples solves the problem, which matters for stochastic generation.
Benchmarks need hidden tests and careful problem design to avoid rewarding memorization or formatting tricks.
humaneval-codex.whyItMatters: HumanEval is the cleanest Phase 0 bridge from language evals to verifiable tasks. It shows why some capabilities should be scored by running code rather than by comparing strings.
humaneval-codex.phaseConnection: Use it to design the first coding eval adapter and to think about when exact-match, regex, and executable checks each make sense.
suggestedReadingFocus: The definition and limits of pass@k
How sampling temperature and number of attempts affect reported capability

helm.oneSentence: HELM argues for holistic model evaluation across scenarios, metrics, and transparency dimensions.
coreIdeas: Models should be compared across multiple metrics, including accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, toxicity, and efficiency.
Evaluation should make prompts, settings, and scenarios explicit enough to reproduce.
A benchmark suite is a measurement system, not just a leaderboard.
helm.whyItMatters: HELM is the best companion for building the Microlab run record format. It pushes us to save configs, prompts, outputs, metrics, and caveats together.
helm.phaseConnection: Use it to shape report metadata, run artifacts, and the dashboard's future result panels.
suggestedReadingFocus: Examples where models trade accuracy against other desirable behavior

big-bench.oneSentence: BIG-bench is a large collaborative benchmark suite built to probe broad and sometimes unusual language-model capabilities.
coreIdeas: A diverse task collection can reveal capability discontinuities and surprising weaknesses.
Task design benefits from many contributors because model behavior is too broad for one narrow benchmark.
Broad suites are powerful, but they require careful aggregation and task-level inspection.
big-bench.whyItMatters: BIG-bench helps Phase 0 stay curious. It encourages small, varied probes instead of only measuring the tasks that are easiest to score.
big-bench.phaseConnection: Use it to justify a mixed phase0-core suite with reasoning, formatting, JSON, factual, and instruction-following tasks.
suggestedReadingFocus: How the benchmark organizes many task types
Examples of tasks that expose non-obvious weaknesses
How aggregate results can obscure task-level behavior

chatbot-arena.oneSentence: Chatbot Arena evaluates chat models through pairwise human preferences and Elo-style ranking.
coreIdeas: Open-ended assistant quality often needs comparative human judgment rather than a single gold answer.
Pairwise preference collection can scale better than absolute human scoring.
Arena scores are useful, but they depend on user population, prompt distribution, and presentation effects.
chatbot-arena.whyItMatters: Chatbot Arena frames the limit of automated Phase 0 evals. It explains why later phases need preference data and qualitative review, not just exact-match scores.
chatbot-arena.phaseConnection: Use it as the bridge from Phase 0 into preference data, reward modeling, and post-training comparisons.
suggestedReadingFocus: Biases introduced by prompt selection and human preference collection
